summary.text: Marine biogeochemical cycles are the pathways that chemical elements and substances follow as they move through seas, oceans and brackish coastal estuaries.
Substances also enter and leave the ocean through exchanges with the air above, the seafloor below and runoff from the land.
Elements cannot be created or destroyed by these processes, so the matter in living things is recycled, while energy flows through and leaves as heat.

facts.label: Main dissolved ions
facts.value: Chloride and sodium, about 85% of all

facts.label: Mississippi dead zone
facts.value: Caused by fertilizer nitrates carried downriver

facts.label: Carrier of everything
facts.value: Water, the medium of all marine cycles

facts.label: Phosphorus to the sea
facts.value: Almost all carried from land by runoff

items.prompt: Farms along a big river spread nitrate fertilizer that washes off their fields. What can this cause where the river meets the sea?

options.label: A dead zone at the river's outlet
Much saltier water along the coast
Nothing, as it settles in the riverbed
Colder water at the river's outlet

items.explain: The dead zone at the mouth of the Mississippi comes from fertilizer nitrates carried off fields and down the river to the Gulf of Mexico.

items.prompt: Sea creatures constantly use nitrogen to build their bodies. Why doesn't the ocean slowly run out of nitrogen atoms?

options.label: The ocean makes new nitrogen from sunlight
Living things create fresh nitrogen as they grow
The atoms are recycled rather than destroyed
Nitrogen is only borrowed for a single season

items.explain: Elements can be neither created nor destroyed by these forces, so they are recycled or stored somewhere on the planet.

items.prompt: Sunlight powers algae, which are eaten by fish, which are eaten by sharks. What happens to that energy along the way?

options.label: It returns to the algae to be reused
It is stored forever in the seafloor
It turns into new chemical elements
It leaves as heat at each transfer

items.explain: Energy flows one way through ecosystems, entering as sunlight and leaving as heat during transfers between feeding levels, unlike matter, which is recycled.

items.prompt: Where does most of the salt in the ocean come from?

options.label: Salty rain falling on the sea
Rocks on land worn down over time
Hot vents on the deep seafloor
Salt made by marine organisms

items.explain: Ocean salinity comes mainly from the weathering of rocks and dissolved salts carried from land, with smaller contributions from seafloor hydrothermal vents.

items.prompt: In a polar sea, a lot of ice melts each summer. What happens to the saltiness of the seawater there?

options.label: It goes up
It stays exactly the same
It goes down
It rises only near the seafloor

items.explain: Melting ice adds fresh water, one of the processes that lowers salinity, while forming sea ice raises it.

items.prompt: Phosphorus worn out of rocks on land ends up in lakes and seas. What carries almost all of it there?

options.label: Dust blown by the wind
Volcanic eruptions
Migrating animals
Water running off the land

items.explain: Runoff is responsible for almost all transport of eroded sediment and phosphorus from land to waterbodies.
